extracted.intended_audience: mathematicians (students, researchers, and authors) who write papers, books, lectures, or other mathematical exposition
extracted.subtask_description: Advice and standards for producing clear, organized, honest, and readable mathematical exposition (papers, books, lectures). Emphasizes planning, notation, iterative rewriting, audience-awareness, and local writing mechanics (grammar, punctuation, symbols, proofs).

rubrics_metrics.name: Say something (have a subject)
rubrics_metrics.description: A piece of writing must have something to say; avoid writing about nothing or trying to say too many unrelated things.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer a clearly delineated, unambiguous subject. Organize around a single subject rather than a mishmash (example: calculus is many subjects and makes bad books). Examples of good works (Nelson's short proof, Dunford–Schwartz) show that length is irrelevant if there's a clear subject. Anti-patterns: long rambling texts with no central idea (Heisel).

rubrics_metrics.name: Speak to someone (know your audience)
rubrics_metrics.description: Decide who you want to reach (diary, friend, specialists, undergraduates) and tailor motivation, informality, detail, and repetition accordingly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specify an audience even concretely (imagine a named colleague). The intended audience affects how much motivation, fussiness, and repetition are required. It's better to aim precisely and miss the target than to aim vaguely and hit nothing. Avoid snide/in-joke remarks that alienate readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Organize first (make an outline)
rubrics_metrics.description: Before writing in detail, devise an outline of main headings, subheadings, what goes under each, and the connections among them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An ideal outline mentions every lemma, theorem, corollary, remark, and proof and orders them to be both logically correct and psychologically digestible. Organization (deciding the graph/tree of topics) is more important than linear arrangement, though both matter. Use a folder of idea slips to prepare. Decide what to include and what to leave out; organize around central examples and counterexamples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Think about the alphabet (design notation early)
rubrics_metrics.description: Invest time early to design consistent, suggestive notation and avoid ad hoc mid-composition decisions that freeze letters or cause dissonance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make tables of symbols and fonts for expected objects (spaces, groups, functions, measures). Avoid 'freezing' common letters for single use (e.g., never always reserve x,y,z) and avoid cryptic acronyms (CW complexes) or frozen designations (property L). Reserve standard meanings (∈ for membership, ε for small quantities) to avoid reader malaise. Bad examples: mixing |z|<ε and z ε U on same page; ambiguous subscripts/superscripts as in Lefschetz.

rubrics_metrics.name: Write in spirals (iterative drafting)
rubrics_metrics.description: Compose and rewrite in a spiral order (1,2,1,2,3,1...) so each new material reveals needed changes earlier parts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: First draft: write freely, violate rules, spill your heart. Rewrite (not mere editing) mercilessly—often whole sections or chapters. Use multiple passes: a full rewrite, then a typescript-ready pass, then proofreading. Avoid merely marking changes with a red pencil; rewrite sentences/paragraphs afresh. Expect early chapters to be rewritten multiple times.

rubrics_metrics.name: Organize always (continuous re-organization)
rubrics_metrics.description: Organization continues during and after writing; use the spiral plan of organization to reintroduce and review earlier material from new viewpoints.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: After introducing a concept and doing it 'right' (motivate, define, give examples/counterexamples), review earlier sections from the new concept's viewpoint. Use subplots and recurring clues (early mention of a word later defined) to prepare the reader. Arrange logically so nothing depends on a later, previously omitted fact. For large works, track dependencies (sheets/numbering) to choose an efficient linear order.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use concrete examples and counterexamples as organizing cores
rubrics_metrics.description: The heart of mathematical exposition is concrete examples and problems; organize work around central, crucial examples and counterexamples.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Big general theories often arise from small insights; readers need guidance in discovering what proofs do not prove. Leave some generalizations for the reader but clearly indicate where a proof fails to apply and provide counterexamples or directions for further study.

rubrics_metrics.name: Write good (correct and unobtrusive) English/local language
rubrics_metrics.description: Exposition should follow correct grammar, diction, and punctuation according to common standards so that the language is unobtrusive and does not distract the reader.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid misspellings and nonstandard reform spelling; know differences like that/which, less/fewer. Aim for clarity, not pedantry: the language should be a transparent instrument. Consult style references (Fowler, Roget, Webster). Bad language accumulates abrasive effects even if it doesn't change correctness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Honesty about status of statements
rubrics_metrics.description: State clearly what is proved, what is unproved, what will be proved later, and your attitude toward claims; do not gloss over difficulties or hide uncertainty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you say 'p does not imply q' and you don't know why, say so. If something is 'obvious', make sure you truly believe it and that others have accepted it; otherwise provide proof, reference, or promise of counterexample. Do not mislead readers about what is known; take the reader into your confidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid irrelevant assumptions and trivial distractions
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not introduce irrelevant hypotheses or fail to treat trivial cases explicitly; both mislead and distract the reader.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example anti-pattern: stating 'If R is a commutative semisimple ring with unit and x,y in R then x^2−y^2=(x−y)(x+y)' introduces irrelevant conditions. Explicitly note or exclude trivial cases (e.g., behavior at 0) when relevant, otherwise readers will feel cheated. In theorem statements, remove irrelevancies and emphasize what's essential.

rubrics_metrics.name: State theorems clearly and early
rubrics_metrics.description: State the theorem (after preliminary definitions/motivations) before its proof; the statement should be as short and direct as possible—one sentence if feasible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid chatter inside theorem statements; move 'Without loss of generality...' and references outside the formal statement. Long multi-hypothesis/ multi-conclusion theorem statements indicate poor organization. The theorem should appear when the reader can best use it to follow the proof and see hypothesis usage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be parsimonious and purposeful with labels and displays
rubrics_metrics.description: Label equations, inequalities, and displays only when a future reference justifies the label; avoid attaching irrelevant labels that waste reader attention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Labels attract the reader's attention; use them sparingly. Anti-patterns: (a) excessive numbering of displays, (b) labels that point to a display on the facing page unexpectedly (Dickson example), (c) inconsistent references like 'g satisfies (1)' when (1) was about f—prefer naming or rephrasing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Write proofs forward (human-readable proofs)
rubrics_metrics.description: Present proofs in a forward, human-manageable order rather than the backwards 'machine-verifiable' way (starting from the desired inequality and working backward).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explain steps in words (a recipe) rather than a chain of equalities that forces decoding. In analysis-style ε–δ proofs, start with an appropriate choice less than ε and proceed forward; this is more graspable. Use typical-case proofs (e.g., prove 3×3 case) when the general pattern is evident, avoiding excessive index manipulation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use symbols and punctuation correctly and consistently
rubrics_metrics.description: Read symbols consistently (e.g., read '∈' as 'is in'), avoid starting sentences with symbols, punctuate symbolic clauses like verbal ones, and maintain consistent verbal translations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer 'If x ∈ A, then x ∈ B' over 'For x ∈ A, we have x ∈ B' to avoid reading ambiguity. Punctuate displays and symbolic sentences as if verbal. Avoid overworked periods/commas between symbol occurrences (e.g., 'Assume that X vanishes. X belongs...' is poor). Use 'then' with 'if' in mathematical contexts to aid readability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance page layout: prose vs displays
rubrics_metrics.description: Design pages to avoid solid prose blocks or overwhelming symbol-laden pages; intersperse displays with enough prose for the reader to avoid drowning in notation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider the printed page while composing. Break dense computations into readable prose or displays at appropriate intervals. Use prose paragraphs as 'recipes' for actions instead of long chains of equalities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adapt exposition to medium (lecture vs paper)
rubrics_metrics.description: Tailor content and omissions to the medium: lectures require stricter omission of computations and faster pacing; papers/books can include more detail and allow readers time to check details.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A lecture's audience has shorter attention and cannot 'pick up the thread' like a reader; in lectures, omit or simplify computations and prepare the blackboard for gradual growth. Treat the live audience's immediate feedback as valuable but plan with oral constraints in mind.

rubrics_metrics.name: Defend your style against mechanical copyediting
rubrics_metrics.description: Be prepared to argue for meaningful stylistic or notational choices when copyeditors or editorial assistants apply mechanical rules that alter meaning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: ensure hyphenation preserves intended adjective forms ('measure-preserving'), and prevent copyeditors from rearranging logical order of phrases. If a stylistic rule (quotation punctuation, comma placement) conflicts with logical clarity, argue for logical placement. The ideal editor who understands mathematics is rare; authors must be ready to defend important choices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be ruthless in rewriting and omission
rubrics_metrics.description: Rewrite fully rather than mark edits; be willing to cut whole sections and to rewrite early material multiple times to achieve clarity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: After a spiral first draft, perform whole-book rewrites, then a typescript-ready pass and proofreading. Wholesale omissions are often necessary—do not hesitate to remove material that impedes clarity. Rewriting means writing again, not merely annotating the first draft.

rubrics_metrics.name: Daily steady production and 'pump-priming'
rubrics_metrics.description: Maintain steady, daily writing progress; end each session by priming the next day's start (plan the first sentence/section title) to overcome inertia.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Write a small bit each day without exception. Prepare the next session by choosing a title or first sentence; this helps keep momentum and leads to completion (Archimedes' small increments).

rubrics_metrics.name: Know when to stop (finish ruthlessly)
rubrics_metrics.description: After proofreading, checking computations, and letting the manuscript 'ripen', stop polishing and send the work; be ruthless about finishing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: There will always be more to add; postpone by ripening, proofreading, and a final read-through for major points (mathematics, exposition, language, format). Once satisfied, stop—further polishing often reveals only mirages of improvement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anticipate reader's difficulties and guide them
rubrics_metrics.description: While writing, continually imagine what will mislead or confuse the reader and take steps to forestall those difficulties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Give motivations, point out where hypotheses are used, promise references or counterexamples when asserting non-implications, and reuse clues/subplots to prepare readers. Avoid statements that leave the uninitiated unsure of status or direction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use reader's aids and indices appropriately
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide lists of prerequisites, preface, index, table of contents, and other aids to help navigation and reader orientation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Add these mechanical reader's aids after major rewrites; they are indispensable for readers and typists preparing final typescripts. Ensure section titles exist (even if not printed) to test unity of sections.
